title: Xarelto and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Rivaroxaban?
excerpt: Can you drink on Xarelto? How alcohol raises bleeding risk on rivaroxaban, why the food rule matters on nights out, how much is too much, and which hangover painkillers to avoid.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Xarelto? How alcohol raises bleeding risk on rivaroxaban, why food matters for your dose, who sets your limit, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol doesn't have a well-known direct chemical interaction with Xarelto (rivaroxaban). It doesn't change your Xarelto levels the way it can change warfarin's effect. But alcohol still raises your bleeding risk in other ways: it irritates the stomach lining, it makes falls and head injuries more likely, heavy drinking can damage the liver that makes your clotting proteins, and binges can set off the heart rhythm problem many people take Xarelto for. There's also one Xarelto-specific catch most articles skip: the 15 mg and 20 mg tablets need to be taken with food to be absorbed properly, and a night of drinking is exactly when people skip dinner. Heavy or binge drinking is a real problem on Xarelto. Whether you drink at all, and how much, is something only your own prescriber can tell you.

**The quick rules:** Never skip or delay a Xarelto dose because you plan to drink. If your dose is 15 mg or 20 mg, take it with a real meal, even on a night out. Only drink if your prescriber says it is OK for you, stick to the amount they set (which may be none), and avoid binges. Don't treat a hangover headache with ibuprofen, naproxen, or aspirin unless your doctor has approved it. And if you hit your head while drinking, get checked the same day, even if you feel fine.

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on Xarelto.** This article explains general research and label information. It is not a substitute for a clinician who knows your health history, why you take Xarelto, your kidney and liver function, and what else you take. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) right away if** you hit your head, especially if you then have a headache, vomiting, confusion, or drowsiness; you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds; you pass black, tarry, or bright red stools; you cough up blood; you have bleeding that won't stop; or you have sudden weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, or vision changes. **Call your doctor soon if** you notice new or unusual bruising, frequent nosebleeds, bleeding gums, pink or brown urine, or unusually heavy periods.

## What Xarelto Does and Why Alcohol Matters

Xarelto is the brand name for **rivaroxaban**, a blood thinner (anticoagulant). It belongs to a newer group of medicines called direct oral anticoagulants, or DOACs. Rivaroxaban blocks a clotting protein called **factor Xa**, one of the central steps your blood uses to build a clot. With that step slowed down, dangerous clots are much less likely to form.

Doctors prescribe Xarelto for several reasons, and the reason matters for how you think about alcohol:

- **Atrial fibrillation (AFib)** not caused by a heart valve problem, to lower the risk of stroke. This is usually a once-daily dose.
- **Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)** or **pulmonary embolism (PE)**, to treat a clot and then lower the chance of another one. Treatment usually starts with a higher twice-daily dose for the first three weeks, then drops to once daily.
- **After hip or knee replacement**, to prevent clots during recovery.
- **Coronary or peripheral artery disease**, where a low dose (2.5 mg twice daily) is sometimes used together with low-dose aspirin.
- **Some hospital patients** at high risk of clots, for a limited period.

Every blood thinner involves the same trade-off. What protects you from clots also makes it harder to stop bleeding. Small cuts take longer to close, bruises show up more easily, and internal bleeding, though uncommon, can be serious. Alcohol matters because it adds bleeding risk from several directions at once, and because it tends to change the habits that keep Xarelto working, like taking it on time and with food.

### How your body handles Xarelto

Understanding a little about how rivaroxaban moves through your body explains why alcohol isn't a direct problem, and where the indirect problems come from.

- **It's absorbed from the gut, and food matters.** The 10 mg tablet is absorbed well with or without food. The 15 mg and 20 mg tablets are absorbed much more completely when taken with food, which is why the label tells you to take those doses with a meal (for AFib, usually the evening meal).
- **The liver clears part of it.** Liver enzymes, mainly one called CYP3A4, break down a share of each dose. A transport protein called P-glycoprotein also helps move it out of the body.
- **The kidneys clear the rest.** Roughly a third of each dose leaves unchanged in your urine, which is why your doctor checks kidney function and may lower the dose if it falls.
- **It wears off within about a day.** The half-life (the time it takes for half the drug to leave your body) is roughly 5 to 9 hours in younger adults and longer in older adults. That's why timing matters: a missed or late dose leaves you less protected fairly quickly.

## Does Alcohol Directly Interact With Xarelto?

Not in any well-documented way. Alcohol isn't listed as a direct drug interaction on the Xarelto prescribing information, and moderate drinking isn't known to raise or lower rivaroxaban levels in your blood. That's a real difference from warfarin, where a binge can push your clotting numbers (the INR) up and long-term heavy drinking can push them down.

But "no direct interaction" is not the same as "no risk." The concerns with alcohol and Xarelto are indirect, and some of them are serious. Think of it this way: Xarelto lowers your ability to stop a bleed, and alcohol raises your chance of having one. The two effects stack.

## The Real Risks of Drinking on Xarelto

### 1. Stomach and gut bleeding

The digestive tract is the most common place for serious bleeding on any blood thinner. Alcohol irritates the stomach lining, and heavy drinking can cause inflammation (gastritis) and contribute to ulcers. On its own, that might cause discomfort. On Xarelto, an irritated or ulcerated stomach lining is more likely to bleed and harder to stop once it starts.

This is worth taking seriously with rivaroxaban in particular. In the large ROCKET AF trial, which compared rivaroxaban with warfarin in people with AFib, major bleeding from the gut was more common with rivaroxaban, even though bleeding inside the skull was less common. That doesn't mean Xarelto is a bad choice. It means your stomach is the place to protect, and alcohol is one of the main things that irritates it.

### 2. Falls and head injuries

Alcohol affects balance, coordination, and judgment. A stumble that would leave a normal bruise can cause dangerous bleeding when you're on an anticoagulant. Bleeding inside the skull is the most feared complication of any blood thinner, and it can start slowly, with symptoms appearing hours after a fall.

This is why the advice is so firm: **if you hit your head while on Xarelto, get checked the same day, even if you feel fine.** Doctors usually want to scan for bleeding after head trauma in people on anticoagulants.

### 3. Alcohol's own effect on clotting

Alcohol has its own mild effects on clotting. Heavy drinking can reduce the number of platelets (the small cell fragments that plug a damaged blood vessel) and make them work less well. That adds to the effect of Xarelto rather than replacing it.

### 4. Liver damage over time

Your liver makes most of your clotting proteins and also clears part of each Xarelto dose. Long-term heavy drinking can lead to fatty liver, alcohol-related hepatitis, and eventually cirrhosis. A damaged liver makes fewer clotting proteins, which raises bleeding risk on its own. The Xarelto label advises against using it in people with moderate or severe liver impairment, or with liver disease that already affects clotting. So years of heavy drinking can eventually change whether Xarelto is even an option for you.

### 5. Triggering AFib

Binge drinking is a well-known trigger for AFib episodes. Doctors sometimes call it "holiday heart," after the spike in AFib cases seen around holidays and celebrations. Regular drinking is also linked to a higher long-term risk of AFib. A 2020 randomized trial published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* found that regular drinkers with AFib who cut out alcohol had fewer recurrences than those who kept drinking.

If you take Xarelto for AFib, alcohol can make the underlying condition worse. Xarelto lowers the stroke risk from AFib, but it doesn't stop the episodes themselves.

### 6. Alcohol is part of how doctors score your bleeding risk

Doctors often use a scoring tool called **HAS-BLED** to estimate how likely someone on a blood thinner is to have a major bleed. One of the items on it is alcohol use, commonly defined as 8 or more drinks a week. In other words, drinking above that level is formally treated as a bleeding risk factor by the people who prescribe these medicines. That gives you a useful benchmark when you talk to your doctor.

## Can You Drink Alcohol on Xarelto?

Only your prescriber can answer that for you. There's no rule on the Xarelto label that says you can't drink, and some prescribers allow an occasional drink for a patient who is otherwise stable, but "can" depends heavily on your situation. Your doctor may tell you not to drink at all if you:

- Have had a stomach ulcer or gut bleed before
- Have liver disease or abnormal liver tests
- Have reduced kidney function
- Are older or have had falls
- Take other medicines that raise bleeding risk, such as aspirin, clopidogrel (Plavix), or regular NSAIDs
- Take Xarelto for AFib and notice alcohol triggers your episodes
- Have had trouble cutting back on drinking

Even if none of those apply, how much and how you drink still matters, which is the next question.

## How Much Alcohol Can You Drink on Xarelto?

There's no official number specific to Xarelto, and the only limit that applies to you is the one your prescriber sets. Here's how different drinking patterns affect risk:

| Drinking pattern | What it usually means on Xarelto |
|---|---|
| None | Lowest risk. Some doctors recommend this, especially with other risk factors. |
| An occasional drink, with food | Sometimes allowed for stable patients, but only your prescriber can say whether that includes you, and how much. |
| 8 or more drinks a week | Counts as a bleeding risk factor on the HAS-BLED score doctors use. |
| Binge drinking (4 to 5+ drinks in one sitting) | A real problem: fall risk, stomach irritation, AFib triggers, and missed or mistimed doses. |

A "standard drink" in the US is about 14 grams of alcohol: roughly a 12-ounce regular beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, or a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits. Many restaurant pours and craft beers are larger or stronger than that, so one glass can easily be closer to two drinks.

The pattern matters as much as the total. If your prescriber allows any alcohol, spreading it out and always having it with food carries much less risk than saving it up for one big night.

## Rivaroxaban and Alcohol When You're Being Treated for a DVT or PE

If you're taking Xarelto because of a recent clot in your leg or lung, the first few weeks deserve extra care. During the first 21 days of treatment, the usual dose is 15 mg **twice** a day, which is a higher total than the long-term dose. This is the period when the clot is most active and when steady protection matters most.

A few practical points for this stage:

- **Consider holding off on alcohol during the first three weeks.** Many patients choose to, and it's a reasonable question to put to your doctor at the start of treatment.
- **Twice-daily dosing is easier to disrupt.** A late night out is a common reason people miss the evening dose or take the morning one hours late.
- **Both 15 mg doses should be taken with food.** Skipping breakfast after a night of drinking undercuts the morning dose.
- **The missed-dose rule is different on this schedule.** The label gives specific instructions for a missed dose in the twice-daily phase that differ from the once-daily rules. Ask your pharmacist to walk you through it so you're not guessing the morning after.

After the first three weeks, most people move to 20 mg once daily, and the general guidance in this article applies. Some people who stay on Xarelto long term to prevent another clot are moved to a lower 10 mg dose.

## The Food Rule: Xarelto's Hidden Alcohol Problem

This is the part most people don't know about, and it's specific to Xarelto.

The 15 mg and 20 mg tablets are absorbed much less well on an empty stomach. Taken with a meal, they work as intended. Taken without food, a noticeably smaller share of the dose gets into your bloodstream. That's why the label says to take these doses with food, and why AFib patients are usually told to take their once-daily dose with the evening meal.

Now think about a typical night of drinking. Dinner gets skipped or replaced with a few snacks. The evening dose gets taken late, without food, or forgotten. The next morning, nausea makes eating difficult. None of that is dangerous in the way a fall is, but it can quietly leave you less protected against clots at a time when your bleeding risk is also higher. It's the worst of both sides.

The fix is simple:

- **Eat a proper meal and take your Xarelto with it before you start drinking**, if your dose falls in the evening.
- **Don't let drinks replace dinner** on nights you take your dose.
- **If you vomit soon after taking a dose**, don't automatically take another. Call your pharmacist or doctor for advice.

(If you take the 10 mg dose, food doesn't affect absorption much, but the timing advice still applies.)

## Never Skip a Dose to Drink

Some people skip their blood thinner on a night they plan to drink, thinking it will lower their bleeding risk. Please don't. Xarelto carries a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest type, that stopping it early raises the risk of stroke and clots. Because rivaroxaban wears off within about a day, a skipped dose leaves you less protected quickly.

If you miss a dose by accident, the general rule on the once-daily schedule is to take it as soon as you remember on the same day, then go back to your normal schedule the next day. Don't take two doses on the same day to catch up. The twice-daily schedule used early in DVT or PE treatment has different rules, so check with your pharmacist. When in doubt, call your pharmacy rather than guessing.

## Side Effects That Can Overlap With Alcohol

Some Xarelto side effects look a lot like ordinary hangover symptoms, which makes it easy to miss a real problem:

- **Dizziness or feeling faint** can come from alcohol, dehydration, or internal bleeding.
- **Tiredness and weakness** can be a hangover, or a sign of blood loss and anemia.
- **Nausea and stomach discomfort** are common after drinking but can also signal irritation or bleeding in the gut.
- **Headache** is the classic hangover symptom, but a sudden, severe, or worsening headache on a blood thinner, especially after any knock to the head, needs urgent care.

A useful rule of thumb: if your "hangover" is worse than usual, lasts longer than usual, or comes with dark stools, vomiting that looks like coffee grounds, unusual bruising, or confusion, treat it as a possible bleed, not a hangover.

## Xarelto and a Hangover: What's Safe to Take

### Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin unless your doctor approves

Ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), and aspirin are the usual hangover painkillers, and they're the riskiest choice on Xarelto. They irritate the stomach lining and affect platelets, so combining them with an anticoagulant and alcohol stacks three bleeding risks together. The Xarelto label specifically warns that taking NSAIDs or aspirin with it increases bleeding risk. Watch for hidden NSAIDs and aspirin in combination products too, including some "hangover" and cold remedies and effervescent stomach products. Our guides to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) explain these risks in more detail.

### Acetaminophen is often the preferred option, with limits

Acetaminophen (Tylenol) doesn't affect platelets or irritate the stomach in the same way, so doctors often suggest it as the go-to pain reliever for people on blood thinners. But it has its own alcohol warning for the liver. Use a single standard dose, stay well within the daily limit, eat something first, and check other products for hidden acetaminophen. If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, ask your doctor first. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) covers the details.

### Non-drug steps help more than you'd expect

- **Water and an electrolyte drink** help with dehydration, which is behind a lot of hangover misery. Staying hydrated is also kinder to your kidneys, which clear part of each Xarelto dose.
- **A bland meal** settles your stomach and helps you take your next dose with food.
- **Rest.** Time is the only thing that reliably ends a hangover.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** More alcohol only delays recovery and adds bleeding risk.

## Supplements, Herbs, and Xarelto

People who drink sometimes reach for liver or hangover supplements. On Xarelto, be careful, because several common supplements can change either your rivaroxaban levels or your bleeding risk:

- **St. John's wort** can lower rivaroxaban levels by speeding up the enzymes and transport proteins that clear it, which can reduce protection against clots. The Xarelto label advises avoiding it.
- **Ginkgo, high-dose fish oil, turmeric or curcumin, garlic supplements, and high-dose vitamin E** are often reported to have mild blood-thinning effects. The evidence varies by product, but it's enough that many pharmacists advise checking before combining any of them with an anticoagulant.
- **Some prescription medicines matter even more.** Certain antifungals, HIV medicines, and seizure medicines can push rivaroxaban levels up or down. Your pharmacist checks for these, so make sure they know everything you take.
- **Anything new**, including hangover and liver-support products, should be run past your pharmacist first. Many contain several ingredients, and few have been studied alongside rivaroxaban.

Bring the actual bottles to your next appointment or pharmacy visit. It takes a few minutes and avoids guesswork.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from combining alcohol and Xarelto if you:

- Are **75 or older** or have had falls
- Have **reduced kidney function**, since the kidneys clear part of each dose
- Have **liver disease**, fatty liver, or abnormal liver tests
- Have a **history of stomach ulcers or gut bleeding**
- Take **other bleeding-risk medicines**, such as aspirin, clopidogrel, NSAIDs, or certain antidepressants (SSRIs and SNRIs)
- Have **AFib that alcohol tends to trigger**
- Are in the **first three weeks of DVT or PE treatment**
- Drink **8 or more drinks a week**, or binge regularly

If any of these describe you, have a short conversation with your doctor or pharmacist before drinking at all. They can look at your full medication list, your lab results, and your reason for being on Xarelto.

## Practical Tips If You Do Drink

1. **Ask first.** Get a clear answer from your prescriber about whether drinking is okay for you, and how much.
2. **Take your dose with a real meal.** For 15 mg and 20 mg doses, food is part of how the medicine works.
3. **Stay within the amount your prescriber set.** Have it with food, never on an empty stomach.
4. **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and helps prevent dehydration.
5. **Never skip or delay a dose** because you're drinking. Set a phone reminder if your dose falls during a night out.
6. **Protect yourself from falls.** Wear sensible shoes, use handrails, light your path at night, and get a ride home.
7. **Plan your morning-after pain relief in advance.** Agree with your doctor on what's safe so you're not deciding while hungover.
8. **Know the warning signs.** Black stools, coffee-ground vomit, or a bad headache after a knock are emergencies.

## Xarelto vs. Other Blood Thinners and Alcohol

If you're comparing your situation with a friend's or a family member's, here's how the main blood thinners differ when it comes to alcohol:

- **Warfarin (Coumadin)** has a direct, well-known interaction with alcohol (see our guide to [warfarin and alcohol](/never-hungover/warfarin-and-alcohol)). Binges can raise the INR and increase bleeding risk, and long-term heavy drinking can lower it. Consistency matters a lot.
- **Xarelto (rivaroxaban)** and **Eliquis (apixaban)** both block factor Xa and have no well-known direct alcohol interaction. The risks are indirect, through the stomach, falls, liver, and heart rhythm. A practical difference: Xarelto is often once daily and its main doses need food, while Eliquis is twice daily and can be taken with or without food. See our [Eliquis and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/eliquis-and-alcohol) for that drug.
- **Antiplatelet drugs** like aspirin and clopidogrel (Plavix) work on platelets rather than clotting proteins (see our guide to [Plavix and alcohol](/never-hungover/plavix-and-alcohol)). Alcohol and aspirin together are particularly hard on the stomach.

For a side-by-side look at all of them, see our main guide to [blood thinners and alcohol](/never-hungover/blood-thinners-and-alcohol).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

You may have found this page while looking for ways to make drinking easier on your body. Here's an honest view for someone on Xarelto.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is in animals and cells, with limited human data. Some lab studies suggest DHM may influence liver enzymes, including CYP3A4, which helps clear rivaroxaban. It hasn't been studied in people taking Xarelto, so nobody knows whether it changes rivaroxaban levels. That's why our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) puts blood thinners in the category that needs a doctor's input first. **If you take Xarelto, don't start DHM or any other supplement without asking your prescriber or pharmacist.**

There is no good evidence that DHM lowers bleeding risk, prevents AFib episodes, or makes drinking safer for someone on a blood thinner. It is not a substitute for drinking less.

If you're reading this for a friend or relative on Xarelto, the most useful thing you can do is help them follow their prescriber's advice: make sure they eat with their dose, have a safe way home, and don't reach for ibuprofen the next morning. For everyone, the habits in our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) matter more than any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol has no well-known direct interaction with Xarelto, but it raises bleeding risk through the stomach, falls, platelets, and the liver, and binges can trigger AFib.
- The 15 mg and 20 mg doses need food to be absorbed properly. Don't let a night of drinking replace the meal you take your dose with.
- Whether you can drink, and how much, is your prescriber's call. Eight or more drinks a week counts as a formal bleeding risk factor.
- Never skip or delay a dose because you plan to drink.
- Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin for a hangover unless your doctor approves. Acetaminophen is often preferred, within its own limits.
- Any head injury while on Xarelto means a same-day medical check. Black stools, coffee-ground vomit, or bleeding that won't stop are emergencies.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Xarelto?**

Only your prescriber can say whether alcohol is OK for you, and how much. Alcohol has no well-known direct interaction with rivaroxaban, but it raises bleeding risk through stomach irritation, falls, and liver strain, and binges can trigger AFib. Your doctor may advise no alcohol if you've had a gut bleed, have liver or kidney problems, are older, or take other bleeding-risk medicines. Ask your prescriber what's safe for you.

**How much alcohol is safe on Xarelto?**

There's no official Xarelto-specific limit, and the only safe amount for you is the one your prescriber sets, which may be none. Eight or more drinks a week counts as a bleeding risk factor on the HAS-BLED score doctors use, and binge drinking is a real problem. If your prescriber allows alcohol, spread it out and have it with food.

**Does alcohol make Xarelto stronger or weaker?**

Moderate drinking isn't known to raise or lower rivaroxaban levels directly, unlike warfarin, where alcohol can shift the INR. Alcohol can still affect how well Xarelto works indirectly: the 15 mg and 20 mg doses need food to be absorbed properly, so skipping a meal or taking a dose late during a night of drinking can leave you less protected. Long-term heavy drinking that damages the liver can also change whether Xarelto is suitable.

**Should I skip my Xarelto dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Xarelto carries a boxed warning that stopping it early raises the risk of stroke and clots, and because it wears off within about a day, a skipped dose leaves you less protected quickly. Take your dose on schedule, with a meal if it's 15 mg or 20 mg. If you miss a once-daily dose, take it as soon as you remember that day and don't double up. Ask your pharmacist about missed doses on the twice-daily schedule.

**Can I drink alcohol on Xarelto for a DVT or blood clot?**

Talk to your doctor first. During the first 21 days of DVT or PE treatment, Xarelto is usually taken at 15 mg twice daily, when steady protection matters most, and many patients choose to avoid alcohol during this period. After that, ask again: your doctor knows your clot history and bleeding risk and is the one to set any limit.

**What can I take for a hangover while on Xarelto?**

Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin unless your doctor approves, since they raise bleeding risk with rivaroxaban. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is often the preferred option, but use a single standard dose, stay within the daily limit, and ask your doctor first if you drink 3 or more drinks most days. Water, electrolytes, a bland meal, and rest help too.

**What are the warning signs of bleeding on Xarelto after drinking?**

Get emergency care for black or tarry stools, vomit that is bloody or looks like coffee grounds, coughing up blood, bleeding that won't stop, or a headache, vomiting, confusion, or drowsiness after any knock to the head. Call your doctor soon for new or unusual bruising, frequent nosebleeds, bleeding gums, or pink or brown urine. If a hangover feels worse or lasts longer than usual, treat it as a possible bleed.

**Is it safe to take DHM with Xarelto?**

It hasn't been studied. Some lab research suggests DHM may influence liver enzymes, including CYP3A4, which helps clear rivaroxaban, so nobody knows whether it changes Xarelto levels in people. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers bleeding risk or makes drinking safer on a blood thinner. Don't start DHM or any supplement while on Xarelto without asking your prescriber or pharmacist.
